title: Can Cyber Operations Be Deterred? What Wargames Reveal
gist: Researchers built an experimental wargame, Tantalus, that separates action selection from action execution with a threat phase in between, making deterrence success directly observable for the first time across 394 games and 1,090 players. The core finding is a paradox: cyber operations can be deterred about as reliably as kinetic attacks, but players almost never bother trying to deter them — meaning states are leaving a working policy tool unused while cyber threats themselves prove weaker deterrents than nuclear ones.

themes.theme: The Unobservability Problem in Deterrence Research

insights.claim: Successful deterrence is definitionally invisible — nothing happens — so conventional empirical methods can observe only deterrence failures (red lines crossed, invasions launched) and never the moment an adversary stands down.
insights.speaker: Ruby Booth and Andrew W. Reddie
insights.so_what: Entire policy doctrines rest on an effect that has never been directly measured — a selection-bias problem that generalizes to any field where the desired outcome is a non-event.
insights.quote: The most successful deterrent threats leave no evidence behind. No missiles fly. No networks go down. No troops cross borders. Nothing happens.
insights.locator: The most successful deterrent threats

insights.claim: When a threatened state takes no action, analysts cannot distinguish successful deterrence from an adversary that never intended to attack in the first place — the counterfactual is unrecoverable from observational data.
insights.speaker: Ruby Booth and Andrew W. Reddie
insights.so_what: Claims that a deterrent posture 'worked' are typically unfalsifiable, which should discount confident assertions about any deterrence-based strategy.
insights.quote: The Republic of Green does nothing. Did deterrence work? Or had they planned no attack? There is often no way to know.
insights.locator: Say, for example, that the Nation of Purple

themes.theme: Why Cyberspace Breaks Classical Deterrence Models

insights.claim: Opacity is the defining feature of cyber operations: states typically cannot observe what capabilities an adversary holds, where malware has been implanted, or whether an intrusion is meant for espionage, pre-positioning, coercive signaling, or imminent attack.
insights.speaker: Ruby Booth and Andrew W. Reddie
insights.so_what: Intent ambiguity means the same intrusion can be read as intelligence collection or attack preparation, which is the structural source of miscalculation risk in the domain.
insights.locator: Now extend this problem to cyberspace

insights.claim: Publicly demonstrating a cyber capability can undermine rather than strengthen the credibility of a threat, because disclosure prompts patching, adaptation, and countermeasures — the inverse of how a missile test builds deterrent credibility.
insights.speaker: Ruby Booth and Andrew W. Reddie
insights.so_what: Cyber arsenals are self-consuming when signaled, so credibility must be built by other means — a fundamental asymmetry against nuclear and conventional deterrence logic.
insights.quote: Unlike a missile test, public demonstration can undermine rather than strengthen the credibility of a threat by prompting patching, adaptation, or countermeasures.
insights.locator: Secrecy further compounds the problem

insights.claim: Because cyber operations are generally less physically destructive than nuclear or conventional attacks, the perceived cost of both launching and absorbing them falls — lowering the threshold for use and changing escalation dynamics.
insights.speaker: Ruby Booth and Andrew W. Reddie
insights.so_what: Low absorbed cost means cyber conflict is likely to be chronic and normalized rather than episodic and deterred — a persistent operating condition for infrastructure operators.
insights.locator: At the same time, cyber operations are generally less

insights.claim: The combination of opacity, attribution difficulty, secrecy, lower destructiveness, and ambiguity of purpose makes cyberspace a poor fit for deterrence models that depend on clear signaling, observable capabilities, and interpretable thresholds.
insights.speaker: Ruby Booth and Andrew W. Reddie
insights.so_what: Imported Cold War deterrence frameworks fail on five independent axes at once in cyber — a checklist for evaluating any proposed cyber deterrence policy.
insights.quote: opacity, attribution challenges, secrecy, lower destructiveness, and ambiguity of purpose make cyberspace a poor fit for deterrence models
insights.locator: Taken together, opacity, attribution challenges

themes.theme: Tantalus: Turn Structure as the Methodological Innovation

insights.claim: Tantalus's novelty is not the inclusion of cyber operations or deterrent-threat mechanics — both exist in prior games including the authors' own SIGNAL — but the turn structure that inserts a threat phase between action selection and action execution.
insights.speaker: Ruby Booth and Andrew W. Reddie
insights.so_what: The measurement design, not the content, is the transferable asset — the same split can expose other unobservable decision moments.
insights.quote: The key novelty in Tantalus is the mechanics of turn structure.
insights.locator: Gaming Deterrence

insights.claim: Because players commit to an action before receiving deterrent threats and can then revise, the experiment records both what players did and what they would have done absent any threat — recovering the counterfactual that real-world observation cannot.
insights.speaker: Ruby Booth and Andrew W. Reddie
insights.so_what: Revealed-preference elicitation before an intervention is a general trick for measuring effects whose success looks identical to inaction.
insights.quote: That revision represents deterrence success, made visible and measurable.
insights.locator: By separating action selection from action execution

insights.claim: The Tantalus dataset spans 394 games and 1,090 players, producing a human-derived large-n sample in a domain where real-world empirical observations are essentially unavailable.
insights.speaker: Ruby Booth and Andrew W. Reddie
insights.so_what: Sample size is what converts wargaming from anecdote to statistical evidence, and it is the criterion to apply when weighing any wargame-based claim.
insights.quote: Across 394 games and 1,090 players, the team could observe not only what players did, but what they would have done had no threat been made.
insights.locator: Across 394 games and 1,090 players

insights.claim: The authors concede the external-validity objection to synthetic environments but argue that models and simulations fare worse because they fail to engage with human decision-making at all, and that the practical alternative to wargame data is no data.
insights.speaker: Ruby Booth and Andrew W. Reddie
insights.so_what: The defense is comparative rather than absolute — the findings should be weighted as the best available evidence, not as settled fact.
insights.quote: To some extent, the alternative to wargaming data is no data at all.
insights.locator: Of course, as with all wargames, there are attendant concerns

themes.theme: Two Definitions of Cyber Deterrence, Two Opposite Results

insights.claim: The phrase 'cyber deterrence' conflates two distinct things — deterring via cyber punishment versus deterring a cyber action by any means — and the ambiguity causes analysts to talk past each other with no clarity on where they actually disagree.
insights.speaker: Ruby Booth and Andrew W. Reddie
insights.so_what: A definitional split that changes the empirical answer's sign — the first question to ask of any cyber deterrence claim is which version is meant.
insights.quote: It is a phrase that can mean many things, leading to many analysts talking past each other
insights.locator: Firstly, it is important to be precise

insights.claim: When cyber is the form of the threatened punishment, cyber threats are measurably less effective than nuclear threats at causing a player to revise a planned course of action.
insights.speaker: Ruby Booth and Andrew W. Reddie
insights.so_what: Cyber retaliation is a weak coercive currency; strategies that substitute cyber response for kinetic or nuclear signaling are buying less deterrence than they think.
insights.quote: cyber threats are less effective than nuclear threats in leading a player to revise their previous course of action
insights.locator: Perhaps unsurprisingly, we find that in this context

insights.claim: The weakness of cyber threats stems from a difference in how cyber punishment is perceived, not from skepticism about whether the threatener actually possesses the capability.
insights.speaker: Ruby Booth and Andrew W. Reddie
insights.so_what: Investing in more demonstrable cyber capability will not fix the gap if the deficit is perceived consequence rather than perceived capability.
insights.quote: the problem is not skepticism about the threatener’s capability, but a difference in the perception of cyber threats compared to nuclear threats
insights.locator: As such, we can reasonably deduce

insights.claim: When cyber is the action being deterred, adversaries are just as likely to be deterred from a cyber operation as from a conventional kinetic attack — actors do not appear to treat cyberspace differently when assessing deterrent threats.
insights.speaker: Ruby Booth and Andrew W. Reddie
insights.so_what: This contradicts significant skepticism in both policy and scholarly communities, and it reframes cyber defense budgets that assume deterrence is impossible.
insights.quote: an adversary is just as likely to be deterred whether they are preparing for a cyber or conventional kinetic attack
insights.locator: Our Tantalus wargame data offers us good news

themes.theme: The Paradox: A Working Tool Left on the Table

insights.claim: Players in the wargame reached for deterrent threats far less often when facing a potential cyber operation than a potential kinetic attack, despite the threat being roughly equally effective in both cases — they appear to resign themselves to the inevitability of intrusions on their networks.
insights.speaker: Ruby Booth and Andrew W. Reddie
insights.so_what: The bottleneck in cyber deterrence is demand-side psychology, not capability — the cheapest available policy improvement is simply making threats that are currently going unsaid.
insights.quote: players seem to resign themselves to the inevitability of cyber operations on their networks
insights.locator: A Cyber Deterrence Paradox

insights.claim: The Department of Defense's 2023 Cyber Strategy asserts that cyber capabilities held in reserve or employed in isolation render little deterrent effect on their own, a position the authors' data directly challenges.
insights.speaker: Ruby Booth and Andrew W. Reddie
insights.so_what: A named official doctrine is being contested with new experimental evidence — a possible leading indicator of doctrinal revision in U.S. cyber strategy.
insights.quote: cyber capabilities held in reserve or employed in isolation render little deterrent effect on their own
insights.locator: This aligns with the perspective taken in the 2023 Cyber Strategy

insights.claim: Policy discourse concentrates on resilience, defense, and recovery while under-weighting deterrence, and a threat that is never communicated cannot influence an adversary's decision calculus at all.
insights.speaker: Ruby Booth and Andrew W. Reddie
insights.so_what: Implies a rebalancing of cyber budgets and doctrine away from pure resilience spending toward declaratory policy — relevant to where defense cyber dollars flow next.
insights.quote: A threat that is never communicated cannot influence an adversary’s decision calculus.
insights.locator: While policymakers frequently discuss resilience

insights.claim: Cyber operations may be less destabilizing and escalatory than originally feared, yet still capable of disrupting military operations, critical infrastructure, and essential government functions.
insights.speaker: Ruby Booth and Andrew W. Reddie
insights.so_what: Lower escalation risk plus real disruptive capacity is precisely the profile that makes cyber attractive for sustained use — expect frequency, not restraint.
insights.locator: Cyber operations may also be less destabilizing

themes.theme: AI Lowering the Cyber Entry Threshold

insights.claim: AI tools and vibe coding are pushing the threshold for entering the cyber domain even lower, which makes credible evidence that casual cyber use can be deterred more valuable than it would otherwise be.
insights.speaker: Ruby Booth and Andrew W. Reddie
insights.so_what: An expanding pool of low-capability attackers shifts the defensive problem from a few state actors to a long tail — relevant to cybersecurity demand and to the case for deterrence over pure defense.
insights.quote: As AI tools and vibe coding push the threshold for entering the cyber domain even lower
insights.locator: The Invisible Made Visible

insights.claim: Experimental wargaming generalizes to an entire class of international security questions whose most important outcomes are definitionally unobservable — deterrence success, escalation avoidance, internal decision calculus, and threats left unsaid.
insights.speaker: Ruby Booth and Andrew W. Reddie
insights.so_what: Signals a methodological shift in national security research; institutions building large-n human-decision datasets gain an analytical edge over model-based competitors.
insights.quote: this is a category of questions in international security where the most important outcomes are definitionally unobservable
insights.locator: Importantly, this is a category of questions
